report.source_text: Direct examination objectified mycelial filaments. The culture after 5 days showed radiated powdery colonies of khaki yellow color (Figure 1). Direct examination of the colony showed terminal and intercalary chlamydospores (Figure 2). Faced with the difficulty of morphological identification, a real-time PCR was performed using the DermaGenius® 2.0 kit (PathoNostics, the Netherlands). Data analysis was performed using the 2nd-derivative and Tm-calling function of the LC480 software (version 1.5.1.62 SP2). This allowed the identification of Epidermophyton floccosum (Figure 3).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 70-year-old immunosuppressed patient (type 2 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis on tocilizumab) presented with fever and painful swelling of the right leg with an erythematous, well-demarcated, warm, tender plaque mimicking bacterial cellulitis. Physical examination revealed concomitant signs of chronic dermatophyte infection including scaly plantar keratoderma and intertrigo of all toe web spaces. Diagnostic workup included direct examination showing mycelial filaments, fungal culture demonstrating radiated powdery khaki-yellow colonies with terminal and intercalary chlamydospores after 5 days, and definitive species identification via real-time PCR (DermaGenius® 2.0) as Epidermophyton floccosum. The patient was initially treated empirically with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and topical terbinafine ointment, then transitioned to systemic therapy with oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 months (ongoing at time of documentation).
